principles.principle: Use a named recurring character, readable expressions and simple compositions to show the problem through action.
principles.application: Lock design and scale, then give each shot one observable emotional change.

principles.principle: A recurring weather metaphor changes with the character from distress toward relief.
principles.application: Track metaphor colour, density and motion alongside character emotion so the transition earns its payoff.

principles.principle: Maintain a coherent illustrated surface, palette and layered environment across shots.
principles.application: Use painterly parallax and restrained movement where they help readability; split location changes into separate shot cards.

principles.principle: Build a consistent miniature world with sculpted surfaces, seams, fingerprints and intentionally uneven motion.
principles.application: Keep material scale, set construction and puppet design coherent; avoid changing to a smooth digital surface between shots.

principles.principle: Small footsteps, prop contact and soft material sounds make the miniature world feel physical.
principles.application: Assign foley to visible contact and reserve a distinct sound for the reveal.

principles.principle: An establishing view can communicate the scale of a miniature scene before closer character action.
principles.application: Choose a wide reveal followed by simpler performance coverage rather than packing every move into one generation.

principles.principle: Select a story structure from the actual audience, offer, evidence and desired outcome.
principles.application: Write one primary angle and a backup; use commercial claims only when supplied evidence supports them.

principles.principle: Turn the selected hook into a timed script and a shot plan covering visuals, dialogue, camera, props and text.
principles.application: Measure a scratch read and resize beats to the requested runtime; suggested source timestamps are examples.

principles.principle: Name a plausible light source and read its direction through the subject and shadows; the source can remain off-screen.
principles.application: Record the source in the set map, then describe how it illuminates the subject from the selected camera position.

principles.principle: Choose hard or soft light for the dramatic intent and use direction to define form and separation.
principles.application: Specify shadow-edge softness, key direction and background separation rather than relying on a cinematic adjective.

principles.principle: Different materials need different visible highlights, reflection and absorption.
principles.application: Describe a few relevant material responses, such as a metal highlight, glass reflection and softer fabric, instead of giving every surface the same gloss.

principles.principle: Anchor source, softness, colour and contrast in the establishing setup and preserve that logic in closer coverage.
principles.application: Carry a physical light map across angles; recalculate screen direction when the camera reverses.

principles.principle: The visual examples distinguish environment-led wide views, gesture-readable medium views, facial close-ups and detail inserts.
principles.application: Choose the information a shot must show: geography, body action, emotion or an identifying detail.

principles.principle: The examples distinguish over-the-shoulder, low, high, tilted, overhead and first-person viewpoints.
principles.application: Choose an angle that reveals the intended spatial relationship or subjective perspective; specify the eyeline and preserve screen geography.

principles.principle: The reference compares wider fields of view, portrait framing, telephoto looks and shallow versus deeper background detail.
principles.application: Describe desired spatial depth and background readability explicitly; lens and aperture numbers are approximate visual cues in generation.

principles.principle: Build spatial depth with foreground, subject-bearing midground and a receding background.
principles.application: Name each useful plane and keep near-camera framing objects from hiding the story action.

principles.principle: Haze, dust or mist can separate distance layers and make space readable.
principles.application: Add atmosphere only when the world and mood support it; preserve the subject silhouette and light logic.

principles.principle: Off-centre placement and existing architectural lines can guide attention toward a subject.
principles.application: Use thirds or symmetry deliberately; direct roads, rails or edges toward the point that matters.

principles.principle: Leave purposeful space ahead of a subject looking or moving across the frame.
principles.application: State the subject position and facing or movement direction; preserve that direction across coverage.
